claim: Human papillomaviruses (HPVs) are the most common sexually transmitted infectious agents.
source: Human papillomaviruses (HPVs) are the most common sexually transmitted infectious agents.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: HPVs have species specificity that prevents study of their natural transmission in laboratory animals.
source: Because of the species specificity of HPVs, study of their natural transmission in laboratory animals is not possible.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HPV biology.

claim: MmuPV1 can cause infections in the female cervicovaginal epithelium of immunocompetent mice.
source: The papillomavirus, MmuPV1, which infects laboratory mice (Mus musculus), can cause infections in the female cervicovaginal epithelium of immunocompetent mice that progress to cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MmuPV1 infections in the female cervicovaginal epithelium can progress to cancer.
source: The papillomavirus, MmuPV1, which infects laboratory mice (Mus musculus), can cause infections in the female cervicovaginal epithelium of immunocompetent mice that progress to cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MmuPV1 is sexually transmitted in unmanipulated, immunocompetent male and female mice.
source: Here, we provide evidence that MmuPV1 is sexually transmitted in unmanipulated, immunocompetent male and female mice.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: One third of female recipient mice acquired cervicovaginal infections from male mice that had been housed with MmuPV1-infected donor females.
source: One third of the female recipient mice acquired cervicovaginal infections.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing 7/22 (32%) recipient females became infected.

claim: Prolonged infections were verified by histopathology and in situ hybridization analyses of both male and recipient female mice at the study endpoint.
source: Prolonged infections were verified by histopathology and in situ hybridization analyses of both male and recipient female mice at the study endpoint.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figures 2 and 3 showing histopathology and RNAscope results.

claim: HPVs are the most common sexually transmitted infection in the United States.
source: Human papillomaviruses (HPVs) are the most common sexually transmitted infection in the United States (Satterwhite et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Satterwhite et al., 2013.

claim: Oncogenic high-risk HPVs account for approximately 5% of cancers worldwide.
source: oncogenic high-risk HPVs alone account for approximately 5% of cancers worldwide (zur Hausen, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to zur Hausen, 2009.

claim: Mucosal tissues of the female reproductive tracts of rabbits are susceptible to rabbit oral papillomavirus (ROPV).
source: Mucosal tissues of the female reproductive tracts of rabbits (Harvey et al., 1998), multimammate rats (Nafz et al., 2007; Nafz et al., 2008), and rhesus macaques (Wood et al., 2007) are susceptible to rabbit oral papillomavirus (ROPV), mastomys coucha papillomavirus 2 (McPv2), and rhesus macaques papillomavirus (RhPV), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harvey et al., 1998.

claim: Mucosal tissues of the female reproductive tracts of multimammate rats are susceptible to mastomys coucha papillomavirus 2 (McPv2).
source: Mucosal tissues of the female reproductive tracts of rabbits (Harvey et al., 1998), multimammate rats (Nafz et al., 2007; Nafz et al., 2008), and rhesus macaques (Wood et al., 2007) are susceptible to rabbit oral papillomavirus (ROPV), mastomys coucha papillomavirus 2 (McPv2), and rhesus macaques papillomavirus (RhPV), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nafz et al., 2007 and Nafz et al., 2008.

claim: Mucosal tissues of the female reproductive tracts of rhesus macaques are susceptible to rhesus macaques papillomavirus (RhPV).
source: Mucosal tissues of the female reproductive tracts of rabbits (Harvey et al., 1998), multimammate rats (Nafz et al., 2007; Nafz et al., 2008), and rhesus macaques (Wood et al., 2007) are susceptible to rabbit oral papillomavirus (ROPV), mastomys coucha papillomavirus 2 (McPv2), and rhesus macaques papillomavirus (RhPV), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wood et al., 2007.

claim: Natural transmission of a papillomavirus through sexual contact has only been reported in rhesus macaques.
source: However, natural transmission of a papillomavirus through sexual contact has only been reported in rhesus macaques (Ostrow et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ostrow et al., 1990.

claim: Cost and lack of suitable molecular biology tools and reagents for rabbit, multimammate rat, and rhesus macaque models have generally deterred their broad scale use.
source: Unfortunately, cost and lack of suitable molecular biology tools and reagents for these models have generally deterred their broad scale use (Christensen et al., 2017; Uberoi and Lambert, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Christensen et al., 2017 and Uberoi and Lambert, 2017.

claim: MmuPV1 (or MusPV1) is a murine papillomavirus that was recently discovered.
source: The recent discovery of a murine papillomavirus (MmuPV1 or MusPV1) (Ingle et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ingle et al., 2011.

claim: MmuPV1 allows the study of papillomavirus infection and disease in laboratory mice, which are tractable, genetically modifiable, and relatively affordable.
source: The recent discovery of a murine papillomavirus (MmuPV1 or MusPV1) (Ingle et al., 2011) alleviates many of these limitations, allowing the study of papillomavirus infection and disease in laboratory mice, which are tractable, genetically modifiable, and relatively affordable.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about laboratory mice and inference from the discovery of MmuPV1.

claim: MmuPV1 infects and causes disease at both cutaneous and mucosal sites of several common strains of laboratory mice.
source: MmuPV1 infects and causes disease at both cutaneous and mucosal sites of several common strains of laboratory mice (Uberoi and Lambert, 2017; Cladel et al., 2015; Cladel et al., 2017a; Cladel et al., 2013; Handisurya et al., 2014; Handisurya et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2017; Joh et al., 2012; Sundberg et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: MmuPV1 infection of the female reproductive tract causes neoplastic disease in immunocompetent FVB/N mice.
source: We recently published that MmuPV1 infection of the female reproductive tract causes neoplastic disease in immunocompetent FVB/N mice (Spurgeon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spurgeon et al., 2019.

claim: The severity of MmuPV1-induced disease is exacerbated by treatment with estrogen (E2) alone or in combination with ultraviolet B radiation (UVB).
source: The severity of disease is exacerbated by treatment with estrogen (E2) alone or in combination with ultraviolet B radiation (UVB), which induces prolonged systemic immunosuppression (Uberoi et al., 2016), leading to precancerous lesions and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Uberoi et al., 2016 and Spurgeon et al., 2019.

claim: UVB induces prolonged systemic immunosuppression.
source: The severity of disease is exacerbated by treatment with estrogen (E2) alone or in combination with ultraviolet B radiation (UVB), which induces prolonged systemic immunosuppression (Uberoi et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Uberoi et al., 2016.

claim: By 4 months following experimental infection with MmuPV1 in their lower reproductive tract and treatment with E2 and UVB, immunocompetent FVB/N female mice develop high-grade precancerous cervicovaginal lesions and SCCs.
source: By 4 months following experimental infection with MmuPV1 in their lower reproductive tract and treatment with E2 and UVB, immunocompetent FVB/N female mice develop high-grade precancerous cervicovaginal lesions and SCCs (Spurgeon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spurgeon et al., 2019.

claim: High-grade precancerous cervicovaginal lesions and SCCs in MmuPV1-infected mice are associated with highly productive MmuPV1 infections throughout the cervicovaginal epithelia.
source: These lesions were associated with highly productive MmuPV1 infections throughout the cervicovaginal epithelia, as evidenced by strongly positive immunohistochemical staining for the major viral capsid protein L1 within the female reproductive tract (Spurgeon et al., 2019) (see also Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spurgeon et al., 2019 and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: All female Donors harbored MmuPV1 infections in their reproductive tracts based upon CVL/PCR tests.
source: All female Donors were found to have MmuPV1 infections based upon the CVL/PCR tests.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MmuPV1+UV+E2-infected mice efficiently establish infections that persist for at least 4 months.
source: This confirmed our previously published results that MmuPV1+UV+E2-infected mice efficiently establish infections that persist for at least 4 months (Spurgeon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spurgeon et al., 2019 and data in the current manuscript.

claim: The infections of female Donors persisted for up to 10 months post-infection.
source: Indeed the infections of these female Donors persisted for up to 10 months post-infection (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 32% of female Recipient mice harbored infections within their reproductive tracts.
source: Using this screening method, we identified 32% (n = 7/22) of female Recipient mice to harbor infections within their reproductive tracts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Of the MmuPV1-positive female Recipient mice, 57% established prolonged MmuPV1 infections.
source: Of the MmuPV1-positive female Recipient mice, 57% (n = 4/7) established prolonged MmuPV1 infections (MmuPV1 positive for at least 2 CVLs)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Of the MmuPV1-positive female Recipient mice, 43% had transient infections.
source: while 43% (n = 3/7) had transient infections (MmuPV1 positive for only one CVL) (Figure 2B, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Prolonging the exposure of male Breeders to both the female Donors and female Recipients from 3 weeks to 8 weeks resulted in a higher percentage of MmuPV1-positive Recipients (50%) than observed in Experiments 1, 2, or 3.
source: Prolonging the exposure of male Breeders to both the female Donors and female Recipients from 3 weeks to 8 weeks in Experiment 4 resulted in a higher percentage of MmuPV1-positive Recipients (50%; n = 3/6) than observed in Experiments 1 (33%; n = 1/3), 2 (33%; n = 2/6), or 3 and 3* (14%; n = 1/7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Preconditioning female recipient mice with Depo-Provera did not appear to influence susceptibility of mice to MmuPV1 infection.
source: Preconditioning female recipient mice with Depo-Provera, a contraceptive drug, did not appear to influence susceptibility of mice to MmuPV1 infection (25% MmuPV1 positive: n = 1/4).
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing similar infection rates.

claim: Co-habitation of female mice experimentally infected with MmuPV1 in their reproductive tracts with uninfected female mice did not lead to transmission of MmuPV1 infections to the reproductive tracts of the latter mice.
source: In a separate set of experiments, we determined that co-habitation of female mice experimentally infected with MmuPV1 in their reproductive tracts with uninfected female mice did not lead to transmission of MmuPV1 infections to the reproductive tracts of the latter mice based on negative CVL/PCR results (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The infections arising in reproductive tracts of Recipient females housed with male Breeders resulted from sexual activity between the males and females.
source: consistent with the premise that the infections arising in reproductive tracts of Recipient females housed with male Breeders (Figure 2A and B) resulted from sexual activity between the males and females.
evidence: This is inferred from the negative co-habitation control experiment and the experimental design.

claim: Of the 7 Recipient females that acquired MmuPV1 infections in their reproductive tract, 6 became pregnant during the course of being housed with the male breeders.
source: Of the 7 Recipient females that acquired MmuPV1 infections in their reproductive tract, 6 became pregnant during the course of being housed with the male breeders (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: The single Recipient female that did not become pregnant had been pre-treated with the contraceptive Depo-Provera.
source: The single Recipient female that did not become pregnant had been pre-treated with the contraceptive Depo-Provera (Mouse #16 in Experiment 3*).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Pregnancy in the Donor females was less penetrant with 4 out of the 7 Donor female mice initially housed with male Breeders having become pregnant.
source: Pregnancy in the Donor females was less penetrant with 4 out of the 7 Donor female mice initially housed with these same male Breeders having become pregnant (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: The lower penetrance of pregnancy in Donor Females likely reflects that they were originally experimentally infected with MmuPV1 using a protocol that involves treatment with Depo-Provera, which can prevent estrus cycling for an extended period of time.
source: This lower penetrance likely reflects that the Donor Females were originally experimentally infected with MmuPV1 using a protocol that involves treatment with Depo-Provera, which can prevent estrus cycling for an extended period of time.
evidence: This is based on inference from known effects of Depo-Provera and the experimental protocol.

claim: No evidence was found for MmuPV1 infections in the skin of several offspring of MmuPV1-positive Donor Females that were screened for E4 mRNA using in situ hybridization.
source: While our analysis was not exhaustive, we did not find evidence for MmuPV1 infections in the skin of several offspring of MmuPV1-positive Donor Females that we screened for E4 mRNA using in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from in situ hybridization analysis.

claim: Recipient #3 had discrete regions of epithelia that were positive for MmuPV1 viral transcripts.
source: Several discrete regions of epithelia were positive for MmuPV1 viral transcripts.
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Regions positive for MmuPV1 viral transcripts correlated with histopathological signs of MmuPV1 infection.
source: These regions correlated with histopathological signs of MmuPV1 infection (Spurgeon et al., 2019), including disorganization of the stratified epithelium, areas of hyperkeratinization, karyomegaly, perinuclear halos similar to koilocytes, and condensed chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Spurgeon et al., 2019.

claim: Evidence for a productive viral infection was observed as indicated by cells staining positively for the viral capsid protein L1 by immunofluorescence.
source: We also observed evidence for a productive viral infection as indicated by cells staining positively for the viral capsid protein L1 by immunofluorescence (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: L1 detection levels were much lower than that afforded by RNAscope-based detection of viral transcripts.
source: albeit at levels of detection that are much lower than that afforded by RNAscope-based detection of viral transcripts.
evidence: This is based on comparison of detection methods shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The infected regions of epithelia in Recipient #3 were pathologically scored as having low-grade or mild dysplasia.
source: The infected regions of epithelia were pathologically scored as having low-grade or mild dysplasia.
evidence: This is based on histopathological analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Recipient #3 was MmuPV1-positive by 6 weeks post-breeding.
source: This particular mouse was MmuPV1-positive by 6 weeks post-breeding
evidence: This is based on CVL/PCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neoplastic disease worsens in MmuPV1 and MmuPV1+E2-infected mice upon extended duration (4 or 6 months).
source: Our previous results indicate that neoplastic disease worsens in MmuPV1 and MmuPV1+E2-infected mice upon extended duration (4 or 6 months) (Spurgeon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spurgeon et al., 2019.

claim: MmuPV1-infected female Recipients may develop moderate to high-grade disease or even SCC if the infection is allowed to proceed for a longer period of time.
source: It is therefore possible that MmuPV1-infected female Recipients may develop moderate to high-grade disease or even SCC if the infection is allowed to proceed for a longer period of time.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on prior results with extended infection duration.

claim: Additional Recipient female mice that were positive for MmuPV1 by CVL/PCR at the endpoint had sites of infections based upon MmuPV1 E4-specific in situ hybridization.
source: We analyzed the reproductive tracts of additional Recipient female mice that were positive for MmuPV1 by CVL/PCR at the endpoint and found them to have sites of infections based upon MmuPV1 E4-specific in situ hybridization (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from in situ hybridization analysis.

claim: Sexual transmission of MmuPV1 can lead to persistent infections in the absence of genetic or environmental manipulation.
source: These results confirm that sexual transmission of MmuPV1 can lead to persistent infections in the absence of genetic or environmental manipulation.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing infections in unmanipulated recipient mice.

claim: Several male Breeders had MmuPV1-positive foci of infection by RNAscope.
source: We identified several male Breeders with MmuPV1-positive foci of infection by RNAscope (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All foci of infections in male Breeders were detected in epithelia of the penis, including the glans epithelium, mump ridge groove, and prepuce (foreskin)/preputial space.
source: All foci of infections were detected in epithelia of the penis, including the glans epithelium, mump ridge groove, and prepuce (foreskin)/preputial space (Phillips et al., 2015; Rodriguez et al., 2011) (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figures 3B and 3C, with anatomical references cited.

claim: Many of the anatomical sites infected by MmuPV1 in male mice are locations infected by HPV in men.
source: Notably, many of these sites are anatomical locations infected by HPV in men (Giuliano et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Giuliano et al., 2007.

claim: Evidence for productive viral infections in the penis was observed using L1 immunofluorescence.
source: We also observed evidence for productive viral infections in the penis using L1 immunofluorescence (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In male mice, L1 was detected at a lower level than that observed for E4 transcripts, which uses the sensitive RNAscope technology.
source: Similar to our observation in the MmuPV1-positive Recipient females (Figure 2D), L1 was detected albeit at a lower level than that observed for E4 transcripts, which uses the sensitive RNAscope technology.
evidence: This is based on comparison of detection methods shown in Figures 2D and 3B.

claim: Two of the male Breeders (Male #3 and Male #5) that had detectable MmuPV1 infections on their penis by the endpoint RNAscope analysis were associated with MmuPV1-positive female Recipients.
source: Two of the male Breeders (Male #3 and Male #5) that had detectable MmuPV1 infections on their penis by the endpoint RNAscope analysis were associated with MmuPV1-positive female Recipients (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Two males that had detectable MmuPV1 infections on their penis did not appear to have transmitted MmuPV1 to Recipient females, based upon CVL/PCR.
source: The other two males that had detectable MmuPV1 infections on their penis did not appear to have transmitted MmuPV1 to Recipient females, based upon CVL/PCR.
evidence: This is based on CVL/PCR data shown in Table 1.

claim: Males that had detectable MmuPV1 infections but did not transmit to Recipients may have had transient infections or their foci of persistent infections were missed by the RNAscope analysis.
source: It remains possible that they did transmit, but the infections in the female Recipients were transient in nature and not caught by the intermittent CVL/PCR tests. Other males that were negative for MmuPV1-infections based upon endpoint RNAscope analysis did transmit MmuPV1 to female Recipients, suggesting they either had transient infections or else their foci of persistent infections were missed by the RNAscope analysis, which is very possible as only one section per male mouse was subjected to in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the limitations of the detection methods.

claim: Of the 4 MmuPV1-positive male Breeders identified using in situ hybridization, only 1 Donor-Breeder mating resulted in pregnancy.
source: Of the 4 MmuPV1-positive male Breeders we identified using in situ hybridization, only 1 Donor-Breeder mating resulted in pregnancy, whereas all 4 Breeder-Recipient matings resulted in pregnancies (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: All 4 Breeder-Recipient matings involving MmuPV1-positive male Breeders resulted in pregnancies.
source: Of the 4 MmuPV1-positive male Breeders we identified using in situ hybridization, only 1 Donor-Breeder mating resulted in pregnancy, whereas all 4 Breeder-Recipient matings resulted in pregnancies (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: MmuPV1 is the first model for studying sexual transmission of papillomaviruses in laboratory mice (Mus musculus).
source: MmuPV1 becomes the first model for studying sexual transmission of papillomaviruses in laboratory mice (Mus musculus).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the study and knowledge of prior literature.

claim: The immediate goals are to use this natural sexual transmission model in immunocompetent mice to study the dynamics of sexual transmission, the role of host immunity, and methods for prevention and treatment.
source: Our immediate goals are to use this natural sexual transmission model in immunocompetent mice to study the dynamics of sexual transmission, the role of host immunity, and methods for prevention and treatment.
evidence: This is a statement of future research directions based on the current findings.
